en: Now, for the purpose of answering the four questions beginning with "Then tell the secret signs" (*atha chommaṃ kathaya*) and ending with "the observation of the omens" (*ityādinimittadarśanam*), he says:
the section from "Then" (*atha*) up to "thus" (*iti*) is the instruction on the secret signs (*chommanirdeśa*).
The section from "The *ḍākinīs*" (*ḍākinī*) up to "for she consists of all the Buddhas" (*sarvabuddhamayohyasau*) is the instruction on the external and internal sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth.

The section beginning with *pīṭham* and ending with *mānavaḥ* is the specification of the ground (*bhūminirdeśa*). The section beginning with *bhraman* and ending with *prajāyate* is the specification of the cause (*nimittanirdeśa*).

In that context, *vāmahastam tu* means "with the left hand"; *tu* is used for emphasis. *Yogī* refers to the *yoginī*; the remainder of the sense is: "swift success arises for the yogin. Alternatively, it is that by which it is known that swift success arises for the yogin.

This is what has been said: For a yogin who is devoted to recitation and meditation, whether he is standing on a seat or the like, or moving about, the yoginīs reveal themselves through signs for the sake of bestowing their grace upon him. The yogin, having perceived their signs, must also perform counter-signs. When they are pleased, they bring about the desired accomplishment. In that regard, the signs of the limbs of the yoginīs are made with the left [hand], while the counter-signs of the yogin are made with the right.

"One finger" refers to the index finger (*tarjanī*). "But she who" means *yā*. The meaning is that this is a question of welcome. "With two" refers to the convention [of using] the index and middle fingers. "One should press the left thumb" implies that this is done with the index and middle fingers. In the same way, the counter-seal (*pratimudrā*) is performed with the right hand. There is a reading in some texts: "one should employ the left finger"; in that case, the meaning is that the index and middle fingers are joined. "The forefinger" (*pradeśikā*) refers to the index finger. Some say it refers to the thumb (*aṅguṣṭha*).

"One should show the ring finger" means one should touch [the neck]; thus [one touches] the neck. "The *paṭṭiśa*" [is formed] by making a fist and extending the index and middle fingers so they are joined; [this is done] by holding it against the forehead. "The trident" (*triśūla*) is formed by pressing the little finger with the thumb and extending the remaining three fingers. "The earth" (*medinī*) refers to the ground. "The teeth," according to some, [refers to the fingers]. "The wheel" (*cakra*) is formed by the thumb and index finger with their tips joined. "The crest" (*śikhā*) is by touching the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*).
"With a ball while playing" means one should show [her] dancing with both hands; that is the meaning.

He says "with the left," etc., because they are to be served by discerning them even through the movements of body, speech, and mind. "With the left" means with the left foot. "Of the *ḍākinī*" is in the nominative case regarding walking and so forth. "From the left" refers to the man. "And speaking with the left hand" means she is habituated to speak while raising her left hand. Some say she makes a loud noise after bowing toward the left.

"One who speaks joyfully to women" means she is one who speaks sweetly to women; "she is called a *samayin*" means she is a female practitioner (*samayinī*). "The request of women" means that one should perform the service of the *samaya* after having entreated them. "By the seeds of the families" means by the seed-syllables of Vairocana and the others.

"Family practice" (*kulakriyā*) refers to the ritual of whichever family she was born into. "He recites his own family" means his own family mantra. "The *vidyā* is always inscribed" means she asks for her own mantra.
"One should draw [the image] in one's own home and take delight" means that "having worshipped" is the ellipsis. "Born from the family of the ḍākinīs" means born from the family of Vajravārāhī.
The passage beginning with "in every land" and so forth is easy to understand.

"Consisting of that *piṇḍa*" means that the body of the yogi has as its nature the *piṇḍa*—the unified convergence in one place—of those twenty-four places such as Pullīra, which are comprised within the ten [categories] beginning with the *pīṭhas*, as well as the goddesses such as Pracaṇḍā, the *khaṇḍas*, the *kapālas*, and their *vīryas* located in those sites. For this very reason, he says "all," and so forth. The sense is that for a yogi of superior capacity (*adhimātra-yogin*), all of this is to be accomplished within his own body alone. It is only by one incapable of internal yoga (*adhyātma*) that one must fall upon external *pīṭhas* and so on (i.e., wander abroad).
This has been stated in the *Śrī-abhidhānottara*:
The elements of those external yogins are depleted through their wandering;
therefore, having rejected the external, one should abide in the play of yoga.
"If they were devoid of reality, nothing would belong to them due to their delusion;
yet if they are endowed with reality, nothing belongs to them due to their delusion. (Abhidhānottara-tantra 65/68)
Furthermore, in the *Abhisamayamañjarī* (ed., p. 18):

"Alternatively, one who has attained proficiency through internal recitation (*japa*), meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and so forth, may undertake a pilgrimage to external sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and other sites at the command of the Goddess. Thus, wandering on the path of conduct (*caryā*) in external fields and so forth is the cause for what is proclaimed as 'internal' [realization]. For this very reason, it will be stated:
'An external yoginī is to be worshipped; [otherwise] the circumambulation of the sacred seats is not possible.'"
Since the ripening of the merit of those to be trained (*vineya*) is of various kinds, there is no contradiction between this [verse] and the previous one.

"Wandering" refers to [wandering] among the seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth. "The sign" refers to that which is surrounded by *yoginīs*. He says that very thing with the words beginning with "various" (*nānā*). Some *yogins* approach in the form of tigers and the like, and in the form of wrathful deities. They laugh with terrifying loud laughter, such as "Hā hā! and so forth. In that situation, the *yogin* must not be afraid. To explain what should be done instead, he says "one's own" (*sva*) and so forth.

The meaning is that, having assumed the form of Śrī Saṃvara embraced by Śrī Vajravārāhī, the sound of the syllable *hūṃ* should be produced. He states this very point with the words beginning "lion" (*siṃha*) and so forth. It should be understood that "seeing and touching" is an elliptical expression, as it includes hearing [the sound] and speaking as well.
This concludes the commentary on the ninth chapter.
